title: Arbitrarily many population maxima under uniform global dispersal
shortTitle: Rare rich patches give population curves many peaks
oneLine: Answering Bai and Li's open question: under uniform global dispersal, total population can have any number of peaks as the dispersal rate varies — the peaks are real but tiny, so the result is qualitative.
abstract: How does the total size of a population depend on how often its members move? In the standard model where individuals leave their location at a fixed rate and resettle anywhere in the habitat with equal probability, Bai and Li (2021) proved that total equilibrium population has a single peak as the dispersal rate varies whenever habitat quality varies by less than a factor of about 1.618, and asked whether several peaks are possible. This candidate shows that they are, in any number. For every N there are smooth, strictly increasing resource functions with any prescribed mean, converging to a constant in every finite L^p, whose population curve has at least N distinct strict local maxima; the mechanism is that a tiny patch of very rich habitat barely changes average quality but adds a population bump at a dispersal rate comparable to its richness. Two resource levels always give exactly one peak, so three is the minimum: an exact three-level example (values 1/20, 25/12, 329/10) has a certified minimum at d = 3, and a second three-level example with contrast about 14.17 is certified exactly and by two rigorous interval traps. The peaks are real but tiny: in the 14.17 example the left maximum lies within 1e-4 of the minimum and is about 1e-32 high, and it vanishes under tiny parameter changes. The result is qualitative. Two close sources (Liang and Zhang 2021; Bai, Li and Shi 2024) were read only as abstracts, so priority is stated within a bounded search. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Any number of peaks: for every a > 0 and N ≥ 1 there are smooth, strictly increasing resources with mean a, converging to a in every finite L^p but not uniformly, whose total population has at least N distinct strict local maxima in the dispersal rate (Theorem 1, proof).

Mechanism: rare atoms of very rich habitat add separated first-order bumps ε r⁻² g_r(d), peaking near d ≈ r/2; each bump gives a population trap that survives the nonlinear problem, smoothing and normalisation (Lemmas 10–12).

Exact example: resource 1/20, 25/12, 329/10 on fractions 2405/3504, 5/16, 1/876 has M(3) = 1, M′(3) = 0 and M″(3) = 6042635/1975192401 > 0, hence two strict maxima; smooth L¹-close increasing versions keep two maxima but not the exact identities (Theorem 2, exact certificate).
Two levels are always single-peaked, with the peak at d = (a + b)/2, so three levels are minimal (Theorem 3, proof).
Low-contrast example: contrast ≈ 14.1734 with two strict maxima, certified exactly and by two interval traps; the optimal three-level contrast lies in [1.618, 14.1734] (Proposition 4).

Effect sizes are tiny: the first peak of the exact example rises about 7.6 × 10⁻⁴ above the dip; in the 14.17 example the left peak lies within 10⁻⁴ of the dip, is about 10⁻³² high and vanishes under tiny parameter changes. The result is qualitative.

narration: Rare rich patches give population curves many peaks. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background: imagine a species spread over a patchy landscape, where individuals leave their spot at some rate and land anywhere in the landscape with equal chance. Ecologists have long asked how the total population depends on that movement rate. In 2021, Xueli Bai and Fang Li proved that, in this well-mixed model, the total has a single peak whenever habitat quality varies by less than a factor of about one point six, and they asked whether it could ever have more than one. Now, the main finding: it can, and in any number. For every number of peaks, there are smooth habitats, arbitrarily close to uniform on average, whose total population rises and falls that many times as movement changes. The trick is a tiny patch of very rich habitat. It barely changes average quality, but it adds a small population bump at a movement rate comparable to its richness. Two habitat levels always give one peak; three are enough for two, and an exact example is certified. As for how large the effect is: the peaks are real but tiny. In one example the extra peak is about ten to the minus thirty-two high, and it vanishes if the numbers are nudged. So the result is qualitative. As for how sure this is: every theorem has a written proof, and the key identities are checked in exact arithmetic. Finally, the limits: review so far is internal and AI-assisted, and two closely related papers were read only as abstracts, so priority is stated with care. This briefing describes version one point zero candidate, released on the twenty-seventh of October 2026; the paper and evidence are linked from the release page. This audio uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional evidence.

decisionObject.description: Answers the question posed by Bai and Li (arXiv:2108.01826, Section 5): under uniform global dispersal the total population can have arbitrarily many strict local maxima in the dispersal rate, with exact three-level witnesses and a proof that two levels are single-peaked.
decisionObject.scope: The uniform nonlocal dispersal logistic model with common quadratic competition; positive bounded resources. Effects are tiny and qualitative; other kernels, patch graphs and the optimal contrast are not addressed.

semanticBridge.description: The model is exactly equation (1.11) of Bai and Li (2021) on a unit-measure habitat; their question is quoted from Section 5, p. 20 of the full preprint.
